intro_hacking.title: What is Ethical Hacking
intro_hacking.introduction: Ethical hacking is the authorized and systematic process of identifying vulnerabilities in systems, networks, and applications to improve security. It involves using the same techniques as malicious hackers, but within a legal and controlled framework.
intro_hacking.detailed_explanation: Ethical hackers use the same tools and techniques as malicious hackers, but they operate with permission. Their goal is to identify weaknesses before attackers can exploit them. Organizations hire ethical hackers to perform penetration testing and security assessments.

sections.heading: Evolution of Ethical Hacking
sections.content: Ethical hacking evolved alongside the growth of the internet. Early hackers were curious programmers, but as cybercrime increased, organizations needed professionals to test and secure systems. Today, ethical hacking is a core part of cybersecurity.

sections.heading: Core Purpose
sections.content: The main goal is to identify vulnerabilities, prevent cyber attacks, strengthen security systems, and ensure compliance with security standards.

sections.heading: How Ethical Hacking Works
sections.content: Ethical hacking follows a structured process including reconnaissance, scanning, gaining access, maintaining access, and reporting vulnerabilities.

sections.heading: Tools Used
sections.content: Common tools include Nmap for scanning, Metasploit for exploitation, and Burp Suite for web testing.

intro_hacking.example: A fintech company hires an ethical hacker to test their login system. The hacker identifies a SQL injection vulnerability, demonstrates its impact, and reports it to the company. The company fixes the issue before attackers can exploit it.

real_world_example.title: Fintech Security Testing
real_world_example.description: A fintech company hires an ethical hacker to test their login system. The hacker identifies a SQL injection vulnerability, demonstrates its impact, and reports it to the company. The company fixes the issue before attackers can exploit it.

intro_hacking.summary: Ethical hacking is a critical cybersecurity practice focused on identifying and fixing vulnerabilities before attackers exploit them. It requires technical expertise, legal authorization, and strong ethical responsibility.

types_of_hackers.title: Types of Hackers
types_of_hackers.introduction: Hackers are individuals who use technical skills to interact with computer systems, networks, or applications. They are classified into various types including White Hat (ethical hackers), Black Hat (malicious hackers), Grey Hat (ambiguous hackers), Red Hat (vigilante hackers), Blue Hat (external testers), Green Hat (script kiddies), Hacktivists (activist hackers), and Nation-State hackers (government-backed hackers).
types_of_hackers.detailed_explanation: Hackers are categorized into White Hat, Black Hat, and Grey Hat based on intent, authorization, and legality. The key difference lies not in skill, but in how those skills are used.

sections.heading: Core Understanding
sections.content: A hacker is not inherently good or bad. The same tools and techniques can be used to secure systems or exploit them. The key difference lies in intent and authorization.

sections.heading: White Hat Hackers (Ethical Hackers)
sections.content: White Hat hackers are cybersecurity professionals who use their skills legally and ethically to protect systems. They work with permission to identify vulnerabilities and improve security.

subsections.title: Example
subsections.content: A company hires a White Hat hacker to test its website security. The hacker finds a vulnerability and reports it, allowing the company to fix the issue.

sections.heading: Black Hat Hackers (Malicious Hackers)
sections.content: Black Hat hackers use their skills for illegal and harmful purposes such as stealing data, causing damage, or gaining unauthorized access.

subsections.title: Example
subsections.content: A hacker breaks into a company database and steals customer credit card information for financial gain.

sections.heading: Grey Hat Hackers
sections.content: Grey Hat hackers operate between ethical and unethical boundaries. They may access systems without permission but typically do not have malicious intent.

subsections.title: Example
subsections.content: A hacker finds a vulnerability in a website without permission and informs the company, sometimes expecting a reward.

sections.heading: Key Concepts
points: Intent defines the type of hacker
Same skills can be used for good or bad
Ethics play a crucial role in cybersecurity

sections.heading: Real-World Scenario
sections.content: In a company system, a White Hat hacker tests with permission and helps fix vulnerabilities. A Black Hat hacker breaks in secretly and steals data. A Grey Hat hacker accesses the system without permission but reports the issue.

real_world_example.title: Three Hackers, One Target
real_world_example.description: In a company system, a White Hat hacker tests with permission and helps fix vulnerabilities. A Black Hat hacker breaks in secretly and steals data. A Grey Hat hacker accesses the system without permission but reports the issue.

types_of_hackers.summary: Hackers are categorized into White Hat, Black Hat, and Grey Hat based on intent, authorization, and legality. The key difference lies not in skill, but in how those skills are used.

legal_basics.title: Legal Concepts in Hacking
legal_basics.introduction: Ethical hacking must always follow legal boundaries.
legal_basics.detailed_explanation: Accessing systems without permission is illegal. Ethical hackers must always have written authorization and defined scope before testing any system.
legal_basics.example: Testing your own system is legal, but hacking another company without permission is illegal.
legal_basics.summary: Permission is the most important rule in cybersecurity.

footprinting.title: Footprinting
footprinting.introduction: Footprinting is the process of gathering information about a target.
footprinting.detailed_explanation: It involves collecting data such as IP addresses, domain details, and employee information. This can be done passively (without interaction) or actively.
footprinting.example: Finding a company email format using LinkedIn.
footprinting.summary: Footprinting helps attackers understand their target before attacking.

osint.title: OSINT
osint.introduction: Open Source Intelligence involves gathering publicly available data.
osint.detailed_explanation: OSINT uses sources like search engines, social media, and public databases to gather intelligence without direct interaction with the target.
osint.example: Finding sensitive information leaked on GitHub.
osint.summary: OSINT is powerful because it is legal and invisible.

port_scanning.title: Port Scanning
port_scanning.introduction: Port scanning identifies open ports on a system.
port_scanning.detailed_explanation: Ports are communication endpoints. By scanning ports, attackers can identify running services and potential vulnerabilities.
port_scanning.example: Using nmap to scan open ports on a server.

network_scanning.title: Network Scanning
network_scanning.introduction: Network scanning identifies devices on a network.
network_scanning.detailed_explanation: It helps map network structure and detect active hosts using techniques like ping sweep and ARP scanning.
network_scanning.example: Scanning all devices in a local network range.
network_scanning.summary: Network scanning reveals the structure of a network.
